question: The last night. What did Jesus want us to remember?
intro: Jesus had one night left with His friends and He knew it. He washed their feet. He broke bread and said "this is my body." He gave a new commandment. He prayed for them out loud. If you had one night, you'd say the things that mattered most. He did. And He told us to remember it every week, which most of us do on autopilot. This week we slow down and figure out what He actually asked us to remember.

days.q: What did He do that night?
days.intro: Two scenes. John gives you the foot washing, which none of the other Gospels include. Luke gives you the sacrament, which John skips. Read both. When you read, notice that in both cases Jesus does something and then says "do this."
days.journal: Jesus said "this do in remembrance of me." When you take the sacrament, what are you actually thinking about? Be honest.

days.q: What was the meal, and what did it mean to them?
days.intro: It was Passover. Every family in Jerusalem was eating lamb and unleavened bread to remember the night God's judgment passed over the houses with blood on the door. Jesus took that meal, the one about a lamb dying so Israel could live, and said the bread was Him now. Nobody at the table would have missed it. Read the original Passover, then read Paul's account of the sacrament, which is actually the earliest one written down.
days.journal: For 1,400 years Israel ate that meal to remember being saved. What are you remembering when you eat yours?

days.q: What did the resurrected Christ say about it?
days.intro: He gave the sacrament to the Nephites too, in person, and explained it more plainly than He did in Jerusalem. Then read the prayers Moroni recorded, which are the same words you hear every Sunday. When you read the prayers, list the promises. There are three you make and one He makes.
days.journal: The prayer says you're willing to take His name, always remember Him, and keep His commandments. Which of the three is hardest for you right now?

days.q: What does an apostle say the sacrament does?
days.intro: Elder David A. Bednar, April 2016. He explains why the sacrament isn't just a reminder. It does something.

read.talk: Always Retain a Remission of Your Sins
read.speaker: David A. Bednar

days.takeaway: His point is that the sacrament isn't a weekly re-baptism, it's how you *keep* the cleansing you already got. He says the ordinance is the Lord's way of letting you always retain a remission of your sins, not just receive one once. Which means what you do on Sunday during those few minutes actually matters, and it's not a passive thing.
days.journal: Bednar says the sacrament is how you *keep* clean, not just get clean. What would change if you treated it that way?

days.q: Should you take it if you're struggling?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. Paul says whoever eats unworthily eats damnation to himself. Jesus told the Nephites not to let people partake unworthily. So if you messed up this week, do you skip it? Most people either take it without thinking or skip it out of shame, and both miss the point. Read these carefully. The word "unworthily" is doing a lot of work and it doesn't mean what most people think.
days.journal: Have you ever skipped the sacrament out of shame? Or taken it without thinking? Which one is closer to "unworthily" in Paul's sense?

days.q: What else did He say to remember?
days.intro: Between the bread and the garden, Jesus said more in one night than in most of the rest of the Gospels combined. A new commandment. The Comforter. The vine. And a prayer for you, by name, in John 17. Read pieces of it. When you read, pick out what He most wanted them to hold onto.
days.journal: John 17:20 is Jesus praying for people who'd believe later. That's you. What do you want Him to have prayed for?

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Next time you take the sacrament, read this first. Then read your Day 1 answer.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: What did Jesus want us to remember? And what will you think about next Sunday?

question: What happened in Gethsemane that didn't happen on the cross?
intro: Most Christians put the whole Atonement on the cross. We talk about the garden too. Why? What happened there that was different? Jesus bled from every pore in Gethsemane before anyone laid a hand on Him. Nobody was hurting Him. Something else was. This week is about what that something was, and what it means that it happened in a garden at night with three guys asleep nearby.

days.q: What happened in the garden?
days.intro: Read Luke, because Luke was a doctor and he's the one who mentions the blood. Then read Mark, who gives you the disciples sleeping. When you read, notice Jesus's exact words in His prayer. He asked for a way out. Then He didn't take it.
days.journal: Jesus asked if the cup could pass. He was allowed to ask. What have you been afraid to ask God to take away?

days.q: What does "Gethsemane" mean, and what was the blood?
days.intro: Gethsemane means oil press. Olives were crushed there under a stone until the oil came out. That's where He went. King Benjamin, 120 years before it happened, described the blood coming from every pore. Isaiah, 700 years before, said the Lord would be *bruised* and that His soul would be made an offering. Read both prophecies, then Luke's verse again.
days.journal: An oil press. The Book of Mormon prophet who wrote about it 120 years early. Does knowing that make the garden feel more real to you, or less? Why?

days.q: What was He actually feeling?
days.intro: D&C 19 is the only place in scripture where the Savior describes His own suffering in the first person. Read it slowly. Then read Alma, who explains *why* He had to feel it: so He'd know how to help you. Then Jacob, on what would have happened without it. When you read, look for the word "every."
days.journal: Alma 7:12 says He suffered so He would "know according to the flesh how to succor his people." What's something you've gone through that you'd only trust someone who'd been through it too?

days.q: What does an apostle say about the garden and the cross?
days.intro: President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, April 2018, Easter session. He walks through the last hours and what they cost.
days.takeaway: His point is that if you want to know who Jesus is, look at what He did in those hours: He chose it. Every step. He could have stopped at any point and didn't. Uchtdorf says the garden and the cross aren't two Atonements, they're one act of love that started in Gethsemane and finished on Golgotha, and the whole thing was for *you*, personally.
days.journal: Uchtdorf says He chose every step. What's one thing you're doing right now only because it's required? What would choosing it look like?

days.q: If the garden was enough, why the cross?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. If He already suffered for sin in Gethsemane, why did He have to die too? And if the cross was the point, why the garden? Read these and figure out what each one did. It's not one or the other. And notice that in the garden He was still calling Him "Father," and on the cross, for a moment, He wasn't. Next week is about that.
days.journal: What do you think the cross did that the garden didn't? Write your answer even if you're not sure.

days.q: How do you actually use it?
days.intro: The Atonement isn't something to admire from a distance. Alma says the Savior took on your infirmities so He could carry them *with* you. That means you're supposed to hand them over. Read King Benjamin on becoming a saint through the Atonement, then Alma's instruction, then the Lord's direct invitation. When you read, look for what you're supposed to do, not just feel.
days.journal: Name one thing you're carrying that you've never actually asked Him to help carry. Ask tonight. Write what you said.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to the garden. Read Luke one more time. Then read what you wrote on Day 7 of Easter week, about why He had to die.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: What happened in Gethsemane that didn't happen on the cross? And has your Easter answer changed?

question: "Why hast thou forsaken me?" Did the Father really leave?
intro: On the cross Jesus said something that should stop you: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" If anyone had earned the Father's presence, He had. And He felt abandoned. Was He? Did the Father actually leave, or did it just feel that way? And if the Son of God could feel forsaken, what does that mean when you do?

days.q: What did He say, and when?
days.intro: Read Matthew and Mark. Both give you the words in Aramaic first, which means it was remembered exactly. Then read the beginning of Psalm 22, because that's what He was quoting. When you read the Psalm, don't stop at verse 1.
days.journal: When have you felt forsaken by God? Write it down. Not the church answer. The actual time.

days.q: Why was He quoting a Psalm?
days.intro: Jews memorized the Psalms. When a rabbi quoted the first line of one, everyone knew he meant the whole thing. Psalm 22 starts with "why hast thou forsaken me" and describes pierced hands and feet and soldiers gambling for clothes, a thousand years before crucifixion existed. But read how it ends. It ends in triumph. Jesus was quoting a Psalm that finishes with God *not* hiding His face.
days.journal: The Psalm He quoted ends with God hearing the cry. Luke says His last words were "Father, into thy hands." What does that tell you about the forsaken moment?

days.q: How far down did He go?
days.intro: The Lord told Joseph Smith in Liberty Jail that the Son of Man had descended below *all* of it. Not most. All. That includes whatever you're in. Read the Lord's words to Joseph, then Paul on Christ becoming a curse, then the Book of Mormon on the depth of it. When you read, look for how low "below them all" goes.
days.journal: "Descended below them all." Is there something you've been through that you don't believe He understands? Write it. Then read D&C 122:8 again.

days.q: What does an apostle say about the forsaken moment?
days.intro: Elder Jeffrey R. Holland, April 2009. He gave this talk about the Savior being alone, and it's one of the most important talks on the Atonement given in your lifetime.
days.takeaway: His point is that the Father's presence *was* withdrawn, at least in some way, so that the Son could experience total alienation from God, the thing sin actually does to us. Holland says it had to be that way so Christ's triumph would be complete. And then he says the part that matters: because Jesus walked that road alone, you don't have to. He's been at the bottom, so there's no bottom He can't reach.
days.journal: Holland says Jesus walked it alone so you never have to. Do you believe that? What's the evidence in your own life?

days.q: How could a loving Father do that?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. If the Father withdrew from His Son at the worst moment of His life, what kind of Father is that? Don't defend Him too fast. Read John 16, where Jesus says He'd be left alone but the Father would be with Him. Read the moment in the garden where an angel came. Read Abraham and Isaac, the only other story where a father walks a son up a hill. Sit with it.
days.journal: Abraham didn't have to go through with it. The Father did. What do you think that cost Him?

days.q: What do you do when you feel forsaken?
days.intro: The Psalm Jesus quoted has the answer built in: God hasn't hidden His face, He heard. Isaiah says God can't forget you because you're engraved on His palms. Alma remembered one thing his father said and it was enough. When you read, look for what each person did with the feeling of being abandoned.
days.journal: Go back to the time you wrote about on Day 1. Was He there? What do you see now that you didn't then?

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to the cross. Read Matthew one more time, then the last verses of Psalm 22, then your Day 1 answer.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: Did the Father really leave? And what does it mean for you when you feel like He has?

question: What does resurrection actually mean for your body?
intro: We say "He is risen" every Easter, but ask most people what resurrection means for *them* and you get a vague answer about heaven. The scriptures are specific. Jesus ate fish. Thomas touched the holes. Alma says every limb and joint gets restored. This is about your actual body, the one that's aging and breaking, and what happens to it. It's more concrete than you think.

days.q: What did the resurrected Jesus look like?
days.intro: Read Luke's account of Jesus appearing in the upper room. The disciples thought He was a ghost. He proved He wasn't by eating. Then read John, where Thomas gets to touch. When you read, notice everything physical about Him.
days.journal: He had a body. He ate. He still had the wounds. What does it mean to you that the scars stayed?

days.q: What did people believe about resurrection before Jesus?
days.intro: Most of the ancient world thought a bodily resurrection was ridiculous. Greeks laughed at Paul for it. The Sadducees, who ran the temple, didn't believe in it at all, and they tried to trap Jesus with a riddle about it. Read Paul getting mocked in Athens, then Jesus answering the Sadducees. When you read, notice that resurrection was a controversial idea, not an obvious one.
days.journal: Job said "in my flesh shall I see God" while covered in sores. What part of your body would you most want restored?

days.q: What does the Book of Mormon say happens to your body?
days.intro: Alma and Amulek are the most specific about it anywhere in scripture. Every limb. Every joint. Every hair. And Alma 40 gives you the sequence: death, spirit world, then resurrection. Read them and write down what's restored and what isn't.
read: 3 Nephi 11:14-15 (the Nephites feel the wounds one by one)
days.journal: Alma 11:44 says restored to its "proper and perfect frame." What's your proper and perfect frame? What do you think gets fixed?

days.q: What does an apostle say about it?
days.intro: President Dallin H. Oaks, April 2000. He's a lawyer and he lays out resurrection like a case. It's clear.
days.takeaway: His point is that resurrection is universal and it's free. Everyone gets it, good and bad, because of Christ, no conditions. And it's *physical*: a body of flesh and bones, with deformities and disabilities gone. Oaks says the assurance of resurrection should change how we treat our bodies now and how we grieve. Death is real but it's not final, and that's not a metaphor.
days.journal: Oaks says resurrection should change how you grieve. Who have you lost? Does resurrection actually help, or does it feel like a distant idea?

days.q: What happens between death and resurrection?
days.intro: Here's the hard part, because nobody knows the timing. Alma admits he doesn't know when resurrection happens for each person. What we do know is the spirit world exists and it's not idle. Read Alma being honest about what he doesn't know, then read Joseph F. Smith's vision of what the dead are doing. Then ask the harder question: what about people whose bodies were destroyed, or who were born with bodies that never worked?
days.journal: Alma says he doesn't know the timing and it doesn't matter. What are you demanding to know about death that might not matter?

days.q: How does resurrection change how you live now?
days.intro: Paul says if this life is all there is, we're the most miserable people alive, because we gave things up for nothing. But it's not. So how do you live like resurrection is real? Read Paul, then D&C 130 on what carries over, then Mosiah on what doesn't. When you read, look for what you keep.
read: Preach My Gospel, lesson 2, "The Resurrection and Judgment"
days.journal: D&C 130 says the intelligence you gain here goes with you. What are you building right now that you'll still have after you're resurrected?

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to the upper room. Read Luke once more, especially the fish. Then read your Day 1 answer.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: What does resurrection mean for your body? Say it plainly, like you'd say it at a funeral.

question: Why did Jesus have to leave for the Holy Ghost to come?
intro: Jesus told His disciples it was better for them that He go away. Better. Than having Jesus in the room. That's a strange thing to say, unless the thing coming next was actually better for them. The Holy Ghost is the part of the gospel most members can't explain. What is He? What does He do? Why is He worth trading Jesus's physical presence for? This week is about that trade.

days.q: What did Jesus say about the trade?
days.intro: Read John 16. Jesus tells them plainly that His leaving is expedient, and then explains what the Comforter will do. Then read Acts 2, when it actually happens. When you read John, list what Jesus says the Spirit will do. There are at least five things.
days.journal: Jesus said it was better for them that He leave. Would you have believed Him? Do you now?

days.q: What does "Comforter" mean?
days.intro: The Greek is *parakletos*, which means someone called alongside you. A lawyer. An advocate. A helper who stands next to you. "Comforter" is a soft translation. It's closer to "the one who has your back." Read the promise He made the night before He died, then Paul on the Spirit speaking for you when you don't know what to say.
days.journal: Advocate means someone standing next to you. When did you last feel like someone was standing next to you when nobody was there?

days.q: What does the Restoration say He actually does?
days.intro: Nephi lays out the order: repent, get baptized, receive the Holy Ghost, and *then* the Spirit shows you everything you should do. That last part is the point. Then read Moroni's list of gifts and the Lord's description of what happens when you have the Spirit as your constant companion. When you read, look for what the Holy Ghost does that nothing else can.
days.journal: 2 Nephi 32:5 says the Holy Ghost will show you all things you should do. Is that your experience? When was the last time He showed you something specific?

days.q: What does an apostle say about receiving Him?
days.intro: Elder David A. Bednar, October 2010. He says the confirmation prayer is a command, not a statement, and that changes everything.
days.takeaway: His point is that when you were confirmed, you were told to "receive the Holy Ghost," and that's an instruction you have to act on continually, not something that happened to you once. Receiving Him means wanting Him, inviting Him, and getting rid of the stuff that pushes Him out. He lists what that looks like: sincere desire, worthiness, and obedience. It's not passive.
days.journal: Bednar says "receive" is a command you keep obeying. What's one thing in your life that's pushing the Spirit out right now?

days.q: Why can't I feel Him?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. You were confirmed. You're trying. And most days you don't feel anything. Is that your fault, His, or is that just how it works? Read Nephi telling his brothers they were "past feeling." Read King Benjamin on what withdraws the Spirit. Read the Lord's warning about what makes the heavens withdraw. Then be honest about which applies to you, if any.
days.journal: Is it possible you've been feeling Him and calling it something else? Or is there something specific keeping Him out? Write whichever is true.

days.q: How do you get Him to stay?
days.intro: Paul lists the fruit of the Spirit, which is really a list of how you know He's there. The Lord tells Hyrum Smith to trust the Spirit that leads to do good, which is a simple test. And Nephi saw the disciples pray for the thing they most desired, and it was this. When you read, look for what you *do* to have Him.
read: Preach My Gospel, lesson 3, "The Gift of the Holy Ghost"
days.journal: Pick one thing from Galatians 5:22-23 you'd like more of. What would you do differently tomorrow to make room for it?

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to John 16. Read Jesus's promise one more time. Then read what you wrote in Week 6 about being born of the Spirit, and your Day 1 answer.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: Why did Jesus have to leave for the Holy Ghost to come? And was it a good trade?

question: Why did God convert Saul, the guy killing Christians, instead of someone nicer?
intro: Saul of Tarsus held the coats while Stephen was stoned. He hunted Christians from house to house. He was on his way to arrest more of them when Jesus knocked him off his horse. And God made *that* guy the greatest missionary in history. Not one of the nice, faithful disciples who'd been there from the start. Saul. Why? What does that say about who God uses, and who's too far gone?

days.q: Who was Saul, and what happened on the road?
days.intro: Read who he was before. He wasn't confused or lukewarm. He was actively destroying the Church and thought he was serving God. Then read the road to Damascus. When you read, notice the first question Jesus asks, and what Saul calls Him back.
days.journal: Jesus asked Saul "why persecutest thou me?" Not "my church." Me. Who have you been hard on that Jesus might take personally?

days.q: How committed was he to being wrong?
days.intro: Saul wasn't a thug. He was a Pharisee of Pharisees, trained by the best rabbi alive, blameless under the law by his own account. He persecuted Christians because he was *zealous*, not lazy. Read his own description of his résumé and what he did with it. Then read Jesus's line about kicking against the pricks, which means he'd been fighting his own conscience for a while.
days.journal: Saul was sincere, educated, and completely wrong. What are you sincerely sure about that you've never actually checked?

days.q: Who's the Book of Mormon version?
days.intro: Alma the Younger. Son of the prophet, going around with the king's sons trying to destroy the Church, and an angel knocks him flat. Same pattern. Read it, then read Alma describing it from the inside years later. When you read, compare the two conversions and see what they have in common.
days.journal: Both Saul and Alma were struck down and couldn't see. Both got up different. Has God ever had to knock you flat to get your attention?

days.q: What does an apostle say about who you've been?
days.intro: Elder Dale G. Renlund, April 2015. He talks about a man who told him "you don't know my past" and what Renlund said back.
days.takeaway: His point is that God cares a lot more about who you are and who you're becoming than about who you were. He quotes a friend who said a Latter-day Saint is a sinner who keeps on trying, and that's the whole definition. Renlund says we have to stop judging people by their worst moment, because God doesn't, and Saul is the proof.
days.journal: Renlund says God cares more about who you're becoming than who you've been. Who's the person you've written off based on who they were?

days.q: Why Saul, and is a dramatic conversion better?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. Most people don't get knocked off horses. They grow up in the Church, feel the Spirit quietly, and never have a Damascus road. Are those people missing something? Paul himself says God chose him as a *pattern*, the worst case, to show nobody's out of reach. And Elijah learned God was in the still small voice, not the earthquake. Read these and figure out whether your quiet faith is less than Paul's loud one.
read: 3 Nephi 9:20 (Lamanites baptized with fire "and they knew it not")
days.journal: Do you secretly wish you'd had a Damascus road? What has your slower conversion given you that Saul's didn't?

days.q: What did Paul do with his past?
days.intro: He never hid it. He told the story of who he'd been in front of kings, in front of mobs, in letters. His past became the proof of the message. Alma did the same thing with his sons. When you read, notice how they use the worst thing about themselves. Then read who was praying for Alma, because somebody was.
days.journal: Mosiah 27:14 says Alma was struck down because his father and the church had been praying for him. Who are you praying for by name? If nobody, pick one and start tonight.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to the road. Read Acts 9 one more time. Then read your Day 1 answer.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: Why did God pick Saul? And who does that mean He'd pick now?

question: Peter's vision. How does the Church change its mind?
intro: For years the Church was Jewish only. Then Peter had a vision of unclean animals and a voice telling him to eat. He said no three times. Then a Roman centurion's messengers knocked on his door, and Peter changed the whole direction of the Church. Not because he wanted to. Because God told him. So how does that work? When does the Church change, and how do you tell the difference between God changing it and people changing it?

days.q: What happened on the rooftop?
days.intro: Read the whole thing, including Peter's refusal. He argued with the voice from heaven. Three times. Then read what happened when he got to Cornelius's house and the Spirit fell on Gentiles before anyone baptized them. When you read, notice how Peter explains it to the Jewish members afterward, and how they react.
days.journal: Peter said "not so, Lord" three times. What's something you'd say "not so" to if God asked you to change it?

days.q: Why was this so hard for them?
days.intro: Kosher wasn't a preference. It was Moses. It was the law God gave them. Jews had died rather than eat pork. Now a voice was telling Peter to eat, and then to go into a Gentile's house, which made you unclean. This wasn't a policy change. It felt like betraying everything. Read the law they were keeping, then read the council that had to sort it out, because it didn't get settled on the rooftop.
days.journal: Acts 15 shows the apostles arguing about it before they agreed. Does it bother you that revelation involved a debate? Why or why not?

days.q: How has the Church changed in our day?
days.intro: The Restoration has its own rooftops. Official Declaration 1 ended plural marriage. Official Declaration 2 extended the priesthood to all worthy men. Both were revelation. Both changed things people had been sure were permanent. When the 1978 revelation came, Black members who'd stayed faithful for years, some for their whole lives, finally received the priesthood and temple blessings they'd been waiting on. Read them, then read the ninth Article of Faith, which is the doctrine that makes change possible.
days.journal: The ninth Article of Faith says God will *yet* reveal many things. What's something you hope changes? What's something you hope doesn't?

days.q: What does an apostle say about leaders and mistakes?
days.intro: President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, October 2013. He said out loud that Church leaders have made mistakes. Then he said why he stays anyway.
days.takeaway: His point is that the Church is run by imperfect people, that things have been said and done that weren't in harmony with doctrine, and that God works through us anyway. He says doubt your doubts before you doubt your faith, and that leaving over the imperfections means missing what the Church actually is. He's honest about the mess and still says come.
days.journal: Uchtdorf admits leaders have been wrong. Does that make it easier or harder for you to follow them? Why?

days.q: How do you tell revelation from culture?
days.intro: Here's the hard part, and it's a real one. Some things the Church used to teach were cultural, not doctrinal, and later got dropped. So how do you know which is which *now*? Paul had to confront Peter to his face about backsliding on this exact issue. Read that. Then read what the Lord says is doctrine versus what people add. Then read the test in D&C 50.
days.journal: Peter, the prophet, was wrong for a while and Paul called him on it. What do you do with the fact that prophets can be wrong on some things and still be prophets?

days.q: How do you follow a Church that changes?
days.intro: The answer is the same one Peter gave: you go where the Spirit says, even when you argued first. The Lord says receive the prophet's word in patience and faith. And in Acts 15 the apostles argued it out, then wrote that it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to them. When you read, look for what protects the Church from changing wrong, and what your part is.
read: Preach My Gospel, lesson 1, "The Church of Jesus Christ Is Restored"
days.journal: Pick one thing the prophet has asked recently that you haven't done yet. Why not? Write the real reason, then decide.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to the rooftop. Read Peter's three refusals and what came after. Then read your Day 1 answer.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: How does the Church change its mind? And how do you follow it when it does?
